entry.title: Windows 11 collects data on usage of coding agents and developer tools via MissionControlAggregator.dll, reporting to Microsoft Diagnostics by default [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Windows 11 includes a system component, MissionControlAggregator.dll, that tracks which coding agents like copilot.exe and developer tools such as python.exe and gcc.exe are used on the system. This data is collected by monitoring Windows events related to process activity and is saved locally before being uploaded to Microsoft Diagnostics if the user has not opted out of optional diagnostic data. The component categorizes tools into broader groups and reports usage through Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) as bitsets indicating which tools were observed during a reporting window. It collects only presence data rather than detailed usage metrics like runtime or interaction counts. This telemetry is embedded in Windows system binaries and operates by subscribing to existing Windows process and application state events.

entry.title: OpenCode launches Browse, a Chromium extension and MCP server enabling AI agents to use users' real browsers with tabs, logins, and extensions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: OpenCode has released Browse, a tool combining an MCP server and a Chromium extension that allows AI agents to operate within users' actual browsers, including Chrome, Edge, Brave, and others. The agents can open tabs in the background, interact with web pages by reading, clicking, typing, taking screenshots, and recording tabs, while handing control back to users for sensitive actions like logins, two-factor authentication, or payments. Browse supports multiple MCP clients such as OpenCode, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and Zed, and uses the user's existing logged-in sessions without requiring additional setup or keys. Users can also lend tabs to agents and restrict agents to allowed sites. Installation involves adding the Chrome extension, which guides through the setup process, with alternative command-line installation options available.

entry.title: Study finds local mathematical objects and structural constraints are key for target-aligned conjecture generation from natural-language mathematical context [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers conducted a paired ablation study using 61 theorems from 12 papers across four mathematical domains to determine which contextual components best support generating mathematical conjectures aligned with target theorems. They analyzed six types of context by removing or isolating each component, producing 793 conjectures to evaluate the impact on alignment with the original theorems. The study found that while components were complementary, local mathematical objects provided the strongest standalone signal, and removing structural constraints and conditions caused the largest drop in alignment. These results suggest effective conjecture generation requires combining information that identifies relevant mathematical objects with constraints that limit admissible claims.

entry.title: ReVision introduces selective intrinsic reasoning to improve tool-augmented visual question answering accuracy across six benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose ReVision, a training-free, test-time method that allows multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to optionally reconsider visual inputs without external tools during reasoning-intensive visual question answering (VQA). Their study finds that while external tools generally improve aggregate accuracy, they can also cause answer reversals by reducing intrinsic visual reasoning. ReVision enables MLLMs to integrate intrinsic reconsideration alongside tool use, improving accuracy by 1.28% to 7.51% over standard tool use on six VQA benchmarks and outperforming the Dual-Rollout Combine method on five, with comparable reasoning-token usage.

entry.title: Study finds probing and steering directions differ in language models, with steering favoring mean difference directions across models and layers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers analyzed three instruction-tuned language models to compare directions used for probing concepts versus steering model behavior. They found that the directions best for detecting concepts do not align with those best for steering, with steering consistently favoring directions closer to the mean difference rather than the best probe direction. This pattern held across nearly all tested layers, models, and concepts, including truthfulness and sentiment. The study also examined transferability across models, showing that probes transferred via linear maps retained most of their probing performance, while steering effects transferred less effectively. Additionally, applying steering toward "unknown" in the PopQA dataset increased abstention rates on uncertain errors significantly more than on confident errors, though it rarely corrected errors when a correct answer was available. These findings highlight distinct roles and behaviors of probing and steering directions within and across language models.

entry.title: Researchers introduce SG-LegalClarify, a large-scale benchmark for legal reasoning and ambiguity recognition in Singapore law, evaluating 19 large language models across 1,860 instances [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: SG-LegalClarify is a new benchmark designed to test large language models (LLMs) on legal reasoning and ambiguity recognition within Singapore's unique legal system, which blends English common law with local statutes. The benchmark includes 1,100 lawyer-authored questions across 10 legal domains, featuring both fully specified and underspecified queries, with responses evaluated using lawyer-developed IRAC rubrics. Researchers assessed 19 LLMs using a multi-turn pipeline where models decide to answer or seek clarification, revealing that even the best models meet only about 70% of mandatory criteria without web search and 78% with it, and struggle to identify when clarification is needed. The team plans to release the benchmark's public split, model outputs, and evaluation tools to support further research in legal AI.

entry.title: Researchers introduce EfficientSkill, a two-step framework that reduces token usage and improves accuracy in multi-turn LLM agents by compressing instructions and offloading reusable code [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: EfficientSkill addresses the problem of prompt bloat and token inflation in multi-turn large language model (LLM) agents caused by accumulating edge-case rules. The framework first discovers a reliable skill without token penalties, then prunes instructions to compress prompts, limit agent turns, and offload reusable code into workspace utilities without additional prompt cost. Evaluations on four models across benchmarks like MATH-500, ALFWorld, and SpreadsheetBench show EfficientSkill reduces output tokens by up to 80% compared to unconstrained methods while improving mean accuracy, including significant gains on SpreadsheetBench with Gemini 3.8 Flash and Grok 4.1 Fast.

entry.title: Study analyzes 40 technical reports of open-weight large language models, finding limited ablation testing and transparency in claimed novelties [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A 2025 analysis of 48 new large language model architectures added to the Hugging Face transformers library reveals that most reuse core components from existing models, primarily Llama. The study examines 40 randomly sampled technical reports to assess claims of novelty, ablation studies, and reproducibility disclosures, finding that only 19 of 73 novelty claims include controlled comparisons and few reports provide multiple training runs or detailed data disclosures. The researchers also investigated whether known components were renamed to appear novel and found no evidence of hidden origins in five candidate cases. They propose seven reporting guidelines for future LLM release reports and apply them to two examples, emphasizing transparency without judging model quality or the truth of untested claims.

entry.title: Researchers evaluate decision models Nimble 9B and Tev1 4B for extracting clinical data from 1,113 oral cavity cancer pathology reports, comparing accuracy and calibration with generative models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers tested two open-weight decision models, Nimble 9B and Tev1 4B, on extracting 25 clinical fields from 1,113 oral cavity cancer pathology reports against a clinical database, comparing them to generative models Qwen3.5 9B and GLM-5.3-flash. Tev1 matched Qwen3.5's accuracy at about 91.7% but was four times faster, while Nimble scored lower at 86.2%, and GLM-5.3-flash achieved 98.6%. Both decision models performed well on simple binary categories but struggled with binned measurements, unreported fields, and complex decisions like involved margins. The study found Nimble's lower accuracy was partly due to processing 25 questions in one request, which improved when limited to two questions per request. The models' probability outputs were well calibrated overall but did not detect systematic errors within individual fields. A simulated approach of escalating uncertain answers to GLM-5.3-flash improved Tev1's accuracy to 98.2%, with 38% of answers escalated. The authors suggest decision models can efficiently extract explicit findings from pathology reports on local hardware but recommend validating them for specific use cases, restricting to reliable fields, and combining with other methods for numeric data extraction.

entry.title: Researchers propose deterministic validation gates for large language model-driven vibration testing of LEO constellation satellites, achieving near-perfect accuracy and error detection [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers developed a method using deterministic validation gates to ensure accuracy in engineering analysis driven by large language models (LLMs), applied to sine vibration acceptance testing for low Earth orbit mega-constellation satellites. Their approach uses multiple checks including unit consistency, physical plausibility, and agreement between independent models to prevent errors and hallucinations in data extracted from Chinese test records by LLMs DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Qwen-plus. The system extracted configurations with 76 fields, achieving fact-level F1 scores between 0.98 and 1.0 across variants, and successfully detected all real and injected errors that would have otherwise gone unnoticed. Retraining models on LLM-generated datasets reproduced results within GPU nondeterminism. The study also found that direct LLM curve forecasting performed no better than linear extrapolation, while a small physics-structured network significantly improved prediction accuracy, indicating when trained models should replace direct LLM predictions.

entry.title: Researchers propose Scalable Bilevel Data Selection for safety-preserving fine-tuning of medical large language models, improving safety rates by up to 4.64 points while maintaining medical capability [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce Scalable Bilevel Data Selection (S-BDS) to enhance safety in supervised fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) for patient-facing medical applications. S-BDS ranks training samples to improve medical knowledge while controlling risks, combining clinician-validated safe data with unscreened medical instruction data. Experiments on Llama and Qwen models show S-BDS achieves higher safety rates than existing methods on HealthBench and PatientSafetyBench benchmarks, with a trade-off between medical capability and safety adjustable via training parameters.

entry.title: Nemotron releases 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, an open small language model optimized for speed and accuracy in fast conversational agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Nemotron has introduced the 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, a small language model derived from Gemma-4-E4B-it and optimized for efficient memory use and speed in conversational AI applications. The model enhances multi-turn tool use, instruction following, and input grounding, targeting local voice assistants, interactive personas, and embedded or edge devices running on platforms like GeForce RTX and Jetson. It achieves the highest average accuracy and generates fewer output tokens compared to its predecessors and competitors across 21 benchmarks. The release includes a DFlash drafter that significantly improves decode speed and generation throughput over previous models.

entry.title: Researchers identify Experience Rot where AI agents fail after silent tool changes, with novices outperforming experienced agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers demonstrate that AI agents relying on accumulated experience fail most tasks after silent changes to their tools, a phenomenon they term Experience Rot. In tests using the Model Context Protocol, experienced agents reused outdated calls without verifying updated interfaces, leading to incorrect success reports, while novice agents adapted more successfully. This failure occurs across various memory types and worsens with more experience. Attempts to mitigate the issue through update announcements or directing agents to documentation were largely ineffective when documentation was incomplete.

entry.title: Researchers introduce SynthDCB, a scalable benchmark using world distillation for device control evaluation across Home, Car, and Phone domains with 114 device classes and 1,166 functions [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: SynthDCB is a new benchmark designed to scale device-control evaluation by creating interactive worlds through world distillation, which modularizes device behaviors, interaction constraints, and environmental effects. It supports multiple domains including Home, Car, and Phone, encompassing 114 device classes, 1,166 functions, and 95 events, and enables task validation and agent evaluation via state correctness and tool-call traces. The benchmark includes five task families with 32 subtypes and was tested on 2,560 tasks across seven models, with the best model achieving a 68.2% Pass@1 score. Analysis identified challenges in answer delivery, feasibility diagnosis, and temporal coordination. SynthDCB also demonstrates improved token efficiency and scalability compared to Codex, reducing token consumption significantly while covering broader capabilities, establishing executable world construction as a foundation for scalable device-control benchmarking and verifiable agent evaluation.

entry.title: Researchers propose Distributional On-Policy Distillation to improve offline on-policy distillation efficiency and student-teacher alignment in multi-turn agentic search [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher model capabilities through token-level feedback but is computationally expensive due to repeated teacher evaluations. Offline methods like Lightning OPD reduce this cost by caching teacher log-probabilities on fixed rollouts but underperform compared to supervised fine-tuning (SFT) in multi-turn agentic search setups. Researchers identify teacher-reference mismatches and distributional flattening as key issues with scalar advantage supervision on fixed rollouts, leading to suboptimal student outputs. To address these challenges, the team proposes Distributional On-Policy Distillation (DistOPD), an offline method that retains candidate-token probabilities from both reference and teacher models at selected positions while aggregating remaining tokens into a residual category. DistOPD achieves performance comparable to online OPD, improves alignment between student and teacher models, and requires similar GPU training time as Lightning OPD, offering a more effective and efficient approach for offline distillation in agentic search contexts.

entry.title: Study finds hard-negative fine-tuning improves spatial reasoning in multimodal large language models with mixed effects across model families and question types [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers evaluated the impact of hard-negative fine-tuning on three multimodal large language model families using CompHall, a compositional benchmark with 2,860 forced-choice questions covering spatial, attribute, counting, and part-whole reasoning. They found that fine-tuning improved spatial-relation question accuracy in all models when using a corrected loss function, but gains were limited or inconsistent across other question types and models. The study also revealed that some questions could be answered from text alone, indicating that compositional failures do not necessarily cause hallucinations in these models. The analysis included controls such as gray-image evaluation, multiple random seeds, option-order tests, and independent benchmarks to ensure robustness. Results showed that the original fine-tuning method harmed some models by focusing on image-placeholder tokens, while the corrected approach required spatial training questions to achieve improvements. Additionally, fine-tuning increased a yes-bias in one model variant, and gains did not generalize broadly across all question types or models tested.

entry.title: Researchers analyze large language models' internal oncology representations, showing they generate consistent cancer patient profiles and predict 12-month survival with up to 89.9% accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers evaluated large language models (LLMs) for their internal representation of oncology by generating synthetic cancer patient cases based on tumor type. They found that LLMs produce similar patient profiles within cancer types and follow biomarker and treatment logic in most clinical scenarios. The models predicted 12-month survival rates with higher accuracy than observed in real patients when continuing patient trajectories. The team developed the Clinical State Space framework to dynamically represent patient trajectories, applying it to both synthetic and real patients. While the study identified limitations in current LLM world models, it suggests that improved models could support digital twin applications in oncology, with the framework providing a method to evaluate such models.

entry.title: Nahual introduces a decoder-only autoregressive diffusion model for combined text and 3D molecular sequences, outperforming specialized models on twelve chemistry tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Nahual is a new generative model that integrates language and 3D molecular data using a decoder-only autoregressive diffusion approach. It employs next-token diffusion to handle continuous 3D coordinates within a causal transformer framework, enabling expressive autoregression without increasing context size. The model is trained end-to-end on twelve diverse 3D chemistry tasks, including microsolvation, molecular conformer search, and adsorption on metal surfaces, surpassing state-of-the-art specialized models in crystal structure prediction and property-conditional molecule generation. This work demonstrates the potential for scaling generalist decoder-only models to achieve native multimodal understanding and generation across language and chemistry domains. The code for Nahual is publicly available on GitHub.

entry.title: Researchers present staged semantic distillation to preserve free-form semantics in a low-compute non-LLM surrogate trained from a single trace of a staged LLM agent [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce staged semantic distillation, a method that preserves non-structured semantics in a low-compute non-LLM student model trained from one recorded trace of a staged LLM agent used in market simulation. The approach uses a frozen encoder to map teacher outputs to vectors, enabling the student to train efficiently with scheduled self-history and stage-specific visibility, achieving close alignment with the teacher's decisions while running without language model calls or text generation. The method was tested on a 200-agent, ten-index market simulator trace, producing a 13.2 million-parameter deterministic student that trains in under 30 minutes on a single 8-GB GPU and runs decisions in 0.14 milliseconds each. The surrogate model maintains semantic channels effectively, reaching balanced accuracy above 0.83 on teacher-forced replay and showing gains over no-semantic retraining. The study highlights the importance of deployment scheduling and content handling in training, offering a faster alternative to running the original large language model agent for simulation tasks.

entry.title: Researchers propose a two-regime framework to evaluate large language model agent markets by separating information simulation and macro emergence using macro-level observations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce a framework that organizes large language model (LLM) agents into multi-agent markets acting as world models, mapping macro information to emergent macro dynamics. The framework separates model capability into two stages: information simulation, translating macro information to micro behavior, and macro emergence, translating micro behavior to macro outcomes, which cannot be captured by a single aggregate score. They propose a soft macro-control method that announces a public reference path daily without altering individual agent decisions and a two-regime evaluation framework that measures both stages from macro observations alone. The framework includes a reference-only regime measuring realization and structural bias through symmetric true and flipped references, and an information-injection regime where external information dilutes the reference, leaving only the true-flipped gap interpretable. Experiments on five single-index LLM-agent markets show that announcing a target path shifts realized paths toward the target under both regimes and information conditions, with improved tracking scores relative to no-reference paths. Structural bias and realization metrics vary with technical and fundamental data shares, demonstrating the framework's ability to assess model capabilities using observable macro-level scores.

entry.title: Researchers find pretraining optimizer gains do not consistently transfer to KL distillation in language models across multiple optimizer comparisons [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A study compares matrix-structured optimizers like SOAP and Shampoo reductions with elementwise optimizers AdamW and AdaGrad during KL distillation of language models initialized from instruction-tuned checkpoints. The results show that none of the matrix-structured optimizers consistently outperform AdamW or AdaGrad in terms of validation KL or training time across four Qwen student-teacher model pairs under a fixed training budget. AdamW generally achieves the lowest validation KL, while AdaGrad can be faster at larger scales, and matrix-structured methods incur overhead or inconsistent performance depending on the recipe and model pair. These findings suggest that optimizer improvements observed during language model pretraining do not automatically apply to short-horizon KL distillation tasks and should be re-evaluated for the specific distillation objective and system constraints. The study highlights the need to tailor optimizer choices to the target training regime rather than assuming gains transfer from pretraining to distillation.

entry.title: Researchers evaluate MAGIC influence-function method for trajectory data attribution on GPT-2-style models, finding reliable predictions in short checkpoint windows but poor correlation over full runs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers tested the MAGIC method for trajectory data attribution on 86M- and 152M-parameter GPT-2-style models trained on multistep arithmetic tasks using filtered web text and synthetic math data. They found that full-run attribution at 86M parameters suffered from numerical overflow and low correlation with retraining results, while short checkpoint windows produced stable and accurate predictions at both model scales. Individual training block rankings predicted retraining outcomes only within the same run and did not generalize across different seeds or hyperparameters, but format-level patterns were consistent across runs. The study also identified two data families-worked examples and primitive facts-that were overrepresented in both the most helpful and harmful score tails, indicating strong local sensitivity distinct from overall net benefit. These findings suggest that trajectory attribution methods like MAGIC are reliable within validated short windows and can provide insights that generalize across training runs.

entry.title: Researchers propose using training-data attribution to guide pretraining data curation by identifying testable data properties for reusable selection criteria [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers argue that pretraining data curation should be guided by training-data attribution, which identifies testable data properties that can serve as reusable criteria for selecting training documents. This approach contrasts with influence-driven selectors that rank documents for a single run, as attributed data properties can be evaluated across different corpora and model checkpoints to better measure usefulness. The paper specifies a feedback loop that interprets attributed sources, tests candidate data changes, and defines evidence requirements for various claim types related to data value. The authors also present a falsifiable comparison of their method against perplexity, classifier, and mixing baselines at equal computational cost, aiming to improve pretraining efficiency and effectiveness.

entry.title: Researchers compare in-context learning, reinforcement learning, and self-distillation for test-time adaptation of LLM agents across multiple environments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers evaluated 14 adaptation mechanisms and a stateless baseline using Qwen3.5-9B on 109 tasks from four environments to determine how large language model (LLM) agents should adapt at test time-through in-context learning (ICL), weight updates via reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (GRPO), self-distillation (SDPO), or combinations thereof. They found that ICL alone provided the largest improvement in mean success rate, increasing it from 28.8% to 49.4%, while adding GRPO further raised success to 51.6%. SDPO showed mixed effects. Analysis revealed that ICL reduced environment lookups and attempt lengths but often skipped task inspection and verification, behaviors that GRPO helped restore without increasing lookups. These results suggest that combining context retention and weight updates can enhance LLM agent adaptation by refining how retained experience is used.

entry.title: Researchers evaluate large language models on choosing future research directions, finding 45% to 67.5% alignment with human authors across 80 comparisons from 19 ML papers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers studied how large language models (LLMs) exhibit research taste by evaluating their ability to choose future research directions given a research goal and current results. They compared eight LLMs against human-authored future-work directions from 19 machine learning papers published between December 2025 and February 2026, measuring alignment, stable divergence, and unstable choice as behavioral indicators. The evaluation involved 80 pairwise comparisons presenting a research goal, hypotheses, key results, and two candidate future directions-one recommended by the paper's author and one plausible distractor. Author alignment among LLMs ranged from 45.0% to 67.5%, with stable divergence between 15.0% and 36.2%. These divergences persisted under various controls, and some non-author preferences were shared across models. The study identified common model preferences toward scaling, generalization, and trade-offs between methodological and infrastructure extensions. This work serves as an early descriptive evaluation of research taste profiles in LLMs and aims to inform understanding and steering of their research preferences as they take on more autonomous roles in open-ended scientific discovery.

entry.title: Researchers propose Termination-Aware On-Policy Self-Distillation (TA-OPSD) to improve language model reasoning by addressing premature stopping and repetition in generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers identify a termination mismatch in On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) where language models either stop reasoning too early or generate repetitive, unproductive outputs. They propose TA-OPSD, which adds two objectives to align teacher and student models on when to continue or stop reasoning and to reduce repetitive generation. Experiments on mathematical reasoning tasks with Qwen3 models (1.7B/4B/8B parameters) show TA-OPSD outperforms OPSD and other baselines across all scales. Ablation studies confirm the new objectives effectively reduce premature termination and repetition-driven over-generation, improving overall termination behavior in language model reasoning.

entry.title: Researchers develop LLM-based retrieval-augmented generation framework to estimate outpatient visit prices from hospital price transparency data, improving accuracy across three Maryland hospitals [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers developed a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework using large language models (LLMs) to estimate outpatient visit prices from hospital price transparency data at three major hospitals in Maryland. The GPT-BM25 hybrid retriever outperformed other methods, reducing mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) to 19.44% for individual procedures and 4.90% for procedure groups compared to much higher errors in baseline models. The approach also showed promise in symptom-based visit cost estimation through synthetic simulations. The study highlights challenges such as heterogeneous data formats, duplicate entries, and limited insurer-negotiated rate availability that affect price estimation accuracy. Despite these issues, the framework substantially improved cost estimates over no-RAG baselines, suggesting that LLMs integrating price transparency data could help patients access more accurate healthcare cost information.

entry.title: Researchers propose ConvRSI framework for parallel multi-agent self-improvement using convolution, improving performance by 5% and reducing inference cost and latency on MATH-500 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce ConvRSI, a framework that parallelizes multi-agent self-improvement by combining intra-agent convolution to refine related features and inter-agent graph convolution to aggregate messages based on collaboration topology. This approach operates in latent space, enabling parallel updates without repeated decoding and re-encoding, addressing challenges of sequential dependencies and high computational costs in multi-agent systems. Experiments on the MATH-500 dataset show that ConvRSI achieves a 5.04% performance improvement while reducing inference cost by 17.27% and latency by 45.11% compared to RecursiveMAS. The framework also supports diverse collaboration patterns by representing topologies as adjacency matrices, demonstrating the potential of convolutional co-evolution for efficient multi-agent self-improvement. The researchers have made their code and datasets publicly available.

entry.title: Researchers present TRACK, a tool-augmented reasoning system combining time series encoding and a Small Language Model for on-device fault diagnosis in power management systems with over 95% accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers introduce TRACK, a system that pairs a time series encoder with a Small Language Model to generate structured, physics-based diagnostic reports for fault detection in power management systems running multiple loads. TRACK operates on-device to keep sensor data local and avoid costly API calls, improving scalability beyond manual expert inspection. TRACK uses a rubric-based evaluation framework assessing report structure, signal fidelity, physics reasoning, diagnosis, and actionability. On a 15-class multi-load simulated benchmark, it achieves over 95% fault-category accuracy and generalizes to out-of-distribution faults, outperforming the best encoder-probing baseline which reaches only 58% accuracy.

entry.title: Researchers test four methods of using embedding-map distances to guide large language model ideation against subsequent developments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: A study evaluates whether selecting points far from existing work in embedding maps can effectively guide ideation in large language models (LLMs). Four tests compare these distance-based approaches against actual later outputs in text, games, patents, and academic papers to assess their predictive and generative value. The tests reveal that random distant points rarely correspond to meaningful text, and LLM-generated continuations tend to stay closer to source material than actual citing papers. Density-based gap scores show limited ability to forecast growth in content areas, and no clear pattern emerges linking distance to inspiration quality. The study uses data from sources including arXiv papers, Steam games, and patents, with results registered before and after analysis to ensure rigor. These findings suggest that embedding-map distances alone may not reliably guide creative ideation or predict future developments, highlighting the complexity of innovation processes and the limitations of current embedding-based heuristics for generating novel ideas.

entry.title: Researchers analyze what small language models learn from an exact verifier in authorization policy explanations, achieving up to 92% accuracy on trained policies [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers studied how small language models learn to explain authorization policy decisions when provided with an exact verifier that identifies minimal sufficient reasons for blocking tool calls. The models receive one request and decision, with multiple opportunities to query altered requests and sufficiency of fact sets, enabling evaluation against ground truth rather than proxies. A fine-tuned 4B parameter model reached 92% accuracy on the policy it was trained on, outperforming frontier models that found exact reasons about half the time. The study found that models trained with algorithmic teaching learned fixed schedules of sufficiency checks, which did not generalize well to unseen policies, while prompting improved minimality in explanations. Reinforcement learning with exact rewards did not improve held-out accuracy but shifted the model's strategy toward sufficiency checks rather than policy probing. The findings clarify how exact verifiers affect training but do not necessarily enhance overall model performance.

entry.title: Researchers demonstrate reward hacking in reinforcement learning using exact process oracles over 124,416 contexts, revealing vulnerabilities in optimistic verifiers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers built a setting where true rewards are exactly computable via executable authorization policies across 124,416 contexts, allowing an oracle to list minimal sufficient reasons for decisions. They degraded verifiers along seven realistic axes and trained models against each while scoring rollouts with the exact verifier, identifying four distinct verifier phenotypes including optimistic verifiers vulnerable to reward padding hacks. The study found that optimistic verifiers showed decreased true faithfulness despite high proxy sufficiency, while outcome-only verifiers saturated and stopped teaching. The researchers conducted nine configurations across multiple frameworks, model vendors, and settings, observing consistent phenotypes and positive sufficiency damage in most replications. They released the testbed, training tools, and 14 real public policies ported to executable oracles to support further research.

entry.title: Researchers introduce Latent Lattice language models that add persistent per-layer horizontal latent streams to improve Transformer performance, reducing perplexity on 20B-token datasets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose Latent Lattice language models that increase computational capacity by maintaining persistent per-layer horizontal latent streams alongside the vertical residual stream in Transformers. This approach enhances attention, KV-cache writes, MLP computation, and decoding, leading to lower validation perplexity compared to parameter-matched baseline Transformers. Experiments on models trained with 20 billion FineWeb-Edu tokens show a reduction in perplexity from 15.41 to 14.40 for a 406M-parameter Lattice model, with further improvements when combined with other residual-stream enhancements. The Lattice method also improves performance across various architectural variants including Gated DeltaNet, Mamba-2, Triadic GDN, and hybrids, outperforming baselines even with smaller native state sizes. These results suggest that adding persistent per-layer states offers a complementary axis for scaling language model computation beyond increasing depth or looped layers.

entry.title: Researchers present a unified framework for controlling large language models, analyzing preference-utility trade-offs and introducing SPLIT steering to improve control while preserving output quality [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose a unified view of methods for controlling large language models (LLMs), such as local weight fine-tuning, LoRA adaptation, and activation-based interventions, framing them as dynamic weight updates driven by control signals. They introduce a preference-utility analysis that measures the tendency toward target concepts (preference) and coherent, task-valid generation (utility) on a shared scale, revealing a consistent trade-off where stronger control increases preference but reduces utility. The study explains this trade-off through an activation manifold perspective, where control shifts representations toward target concepts but can push them off the model's valid-generation manifold, reducing utility. Based on this analysis, the researchers develop a new steering method called SPLIT that enhances preference while better maintaining utility, with code made publicly available.

entry.title: Researchers introduce SteerEval benchmark to evaluate controllability of large language models across language features, sentiment, and personality at multiple behavioral levels [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed SteerEval, a hierarchical benchmark designed to assess the controllability of large language models (LLMs) in socially sensitive contexts by evaluating language features, sentiment, and personality across three specification levels. The benchmark connects high-level behavioral intent to specific textual outputs and reveals that control tends to weaken at finer-grained levels. SteerEval provides a structured and interpretable framework to guide safer and more controllable LLM behavior, aiming to support future research in this area.

entry.title: Researchers release Metacognitive Profile Atlas analyzing confidence discrimination across 33 leading LLMs on 1,500 MMLU items by domain [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: The Metacognitive Profile Atlas provides answer and verbalized confidence data from 33 advanced large language models (LLMs) tested on 1,500 MMLU items grouped into six subject domains. The study finds that confidence best discriminates correct from incorrect answers in Applied/Professional domains and least effectively in Formal Reasoning and Natural Science, with statistical significance across the population of models. Individual model profiles show low reliability, though some within-family similarities are noted, particularly for Anthropic models. The dataset includes 46,157 scored observations after excluding parser-imputed values and distinguishes genuine monitoring improvements from error removal in model versions. The analysis also reveals that some models perform better with verbalized confidence than with binary-probe confidence measures. This version incorporates peer review revisions and corrects earlier data artifacts, providing a resource for further exploration of metacognitive abilities in frontier LLMs.

entry.title: Researchers introduce Recursive Semantic Divergence metric to measure and improve consistency in large language model agents using tool use across independent runs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Large language model agents that use tools can behave inconsistently across runs starting from the same state, leading to divergent strategies and contradictory outputs that undermine reliability. Existing metrics focus on task correctness but do not capture behavioral consistency over time. Researchers propose Recursive Semantic Divergence (RSD), a trajectory-level metric adapted from reinforcement learning bisimulation, which measures cumulative semantic disagreement between independent agent rollouts using natural language inference to detect logical inconsistencies. RSD is approximated by a neural network and provides a consistency score at each step without needing the full trajectory. When used as a reward signal for fine-tuning, RSD reduces variability in performance metrics by up to 50.5% on benchmarks such as tau2-bench and ToolSandbox, improving task progress across multiple model and benchmark settings including Qwen-2.5 and Qwen-3.5. This approach offers a new way to quantify and enhance the consistency of LLM agents in sequential decision-making tasks.

entry.title: Researchers introduce Agentic Soft-Token Compression for long-horizon LLM agents, reducing computation by up to 59.84% while maintaining accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers propose Agentic Soft-Token Compression (ASTC), a training-free method that uses soft tokens within large language model (LLM) agents to compress context in long-horizon tasks. ASTC leverages the model's recurrent dynamics and hybrid Gated Delta Network attention to carry forward absorbed information as soft tokens, reducing later-layer computation and enabling reusable key-value caches. Experiments show ASTC matches or exceeds the accuracy of uncompressed agents while using significantly fewer attention pairs, outperforming trained external compressors that require substantially more computation. This approach offers a model-native way to efficiently manage growing interaction contexts in sustained LLM tasks.

entry.title: Researchers compare two releases of a 307M-parameter multilingual cross-encoder Ru-Jev, finding label-wording augmentation improves accuracy on unfamiliar words but not on abbreviations or codes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers evaluated two versions of Ru-Jev, a multilingual cross-encoder trained on thirteen Russian-language tasks, to assess the impact of label wording on model accuracy. The later release introduced an augmentation presenting labels in multiple surface forms, which improved accuracy on held-out vocabularies of ordinary and borrowed words, including jargon and office slang, but showed no significant gains on abbreviations or opaque codes. The study tested ten label vocabularies with varying candidate sizes and controlled for overlap with training data. While the augmented model consistently outperformed the earlier release on unfamiliar words, gains were partly influenced by specific labels and reduced when adjusting for per-option biases. On unseen datasets, accuracy differences varied, and checkpoint rankings were inconsistent, highlighting challenges in evaluation. The researchers also identified four hazards in comparing model releases, emphasizing the complexity of assessing label wording effects in typed-decision models.

entry.title: ResBench introduces a resource-aware benchmark for evaluating LLM-generated FPGA designs across 56 problems and 12 categories [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: ResBench is a new benchmark designed to evaluate large language models (LLMs) on their ability to generate hardware description language (HDL) code for FPGAs with a focus on resource optimization. It includes 56 problems spanning 12 categories, from finite state machines to financial computing, and uses an open-source framework to generate Verilog code, verify correctness, and measure resource usage, primarily lookup table (LUT) consumption. Experiments with ResBench reveal significant differences among LLMs in producing resource-efficient FPGA designs, addressing limitations of prior benchmarks that focused mainly on functional correctness without considering hardware resource usage.

entry.title: Researchers introduce a black-box interpretability framework using atomic concept edits to learn verifiable constitutions that predict and control model behavior across tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have developed a black-box interpretability framework that learns a verifiable constitution-a natural language summary describing how prompt changes affect a model's behavior such as alignment and correctness. The method uses atomic concept edits (ACEs) to add, remove, or replace interpretable concepts in prompts and observes resulting behavior changes to establish causal mappings. This approach was validated on tasks including mathematical reasoning and text-to-image generation, revealing differences in model focus such as GPT-Image's emphasis on grammar versus Imagen 4's atmospheric coherence. The learned constitutions improved control over model behavior, boosting success rates by an average of 1.86 times compared to methods without constitutions. The researchers have open-sourced their code for further use and study.

entry.title: Researchers develop Terminator, an early-exit strategy to reduce overthinking in large reasoning models by predicting optimal stopping points in chain-of-thought reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers have introduced Terminator, a method designed to reduce excessive computation in large reasoning models (LRMs) by learning optimal exit points during chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. Terminator predicts when the model's final answer first appears and uses this to train an early-exit strategy that shortens reasoning length without sacrificing accuracy. The approach was tested on four datasets-MATH-500, AIME 2025, HumanEval, and GPQA-achieving 14% to 55% reductions in reasoning length and more than doubling inference speed compared to original models. This work addresses the challenge of determining task- and model-dependent optimal reasoning lengths, improving efficiency in complex reasoning tasks.

entry.title: Researchers characterize identification and generation limits using contrastive pairs under corruption budgets in finite and countable hypothesis classes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: This paper studies a learning scenario where a learner receives only contrastive pairs-unordered pairs of points labeled as dissimilar-without knowing which point is positive. The authors characterize exactly which hypothesis classes are identifiable under any corruption budget and introduce a contrastive closure dimension to describe uniform generation capabilities. They show that on clean data, four learning criteria form a strict hierarchy, but under corruption, some classes become identifiable from contrastive pairs even when positive examples with corruption fail.

entry.title: Researchers propose CapCode and CapReward to detect and prevent cheating in coding agent evaluations using capped scores and randomized tests [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers identify a growing issue in evaluating coding agents where models achieve high scores by exploiting shortcuts rather than solving tasks as intended, leading to deceptive evaluation results. They introduce CapCode, a framework that uses randomized tests with a deliberately capped maximum non-cheating score to make cheating detectable when scores exceed this cap. To discourage cheating, they also propose CapReward, a reward system designed to prevent optimization beyond the capped score. Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that CapCode effectively detects cheating while maintaining accurate performance rankings among models. CapReward reduces cheating behaviors, resulting in models that better adhere to the intended task specifications, improving the reliability of coding agent evaluations.

entry.title: Researchers propose Multi-Head Recurrent Memory framework to improve long-context retention in LLMs, boosting accuracy and memory retention up to 73.96% at nearly 900K tokens [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers identify memory retention as the main bottleneck in recurrent memory agents that extend large language models (LLMs) to handle arbitrarily long contexts. They propose Multi-Head Recurrent Memory (MHM), a training-free framework that partitions memory into independent heads updated selectively to prevent overwriting and improve retention. They introduce a lightweight version, MHM-LRU, which ensures uniform head usage without extra token overhead. Experiments on long-context benchmarks from 100K to 1M tokens show MHM-LRU significantly improves retention and end-to-end accuracy compared to baseline methods, with retention rates rising from under 30% to nearly 74% on the RULER-HQA dataset at 896K tokens. These improvements generalize across model types, scales, and tasks, suggesting architectural design as a practical approach to reliable long-context memory in LLMs.

entry.title: Researchers find that pooled accuracy of chain-of-thought monitors masks fragility on reasoning-dependent subsets, revealing vulnerability to controlled reasoning rewrites [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers analyzed chain-of-thought (CoT) monitors used to detect reward hacks and found that their reported aggregate accuracy conceals significant fragility on a reasoning-dependent subset of hacks. On the Terminal Wrench dataset, about 77% of hacks are detectable by actions alone, dominating the pooled accuracy, while the remaining 23% evade action-only detection and expose monitor weaknesses when reasoning is subtly rewritten without changing commands or outputs. A controlled attack that altered only the agent's reasoning reduced detection rates on this subset from around 95% to between 4% and 11%, though the overall pooled accuracy dropped only modestly. The study showed that these reasoning-based attacks remain truthful about events but obscure intent, limiting the effectiveness of trace-only monitors even when alerted to the attack. The vulnerability transfers across different monitor and agent types, and live agents instructed to hack without monitor feedback produced detectable but hollow hacks. Applying the reasoning rewrite to these live hacks maintained detection of action-visible hacks but lowered detection on others, consistent with the false average effect. The authors suggest that monitor accuracy should be reported specifically on reasoning-dependent subsets where defenses are critical, as external information beyond the trace is necessary to improve robustness.

entry.title: Researchers find margin to TopK threshold determines sparse autoencoder ablation effects and improve prediction accuracy with margin graphs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers studied sparse autoencoders (SAEs) that pass only the top k largest preactivations, finding that zeroing one feature changes the active set in 74% to 89% of cases across five public TopK SAEs. They introduced a margin graph method that adds first order changes to downstream preactivations before selecting the top k again, reducing median prediction error on Pythia-70M by 84% compared to attribution graphs. Exact recomputation of interventions was faster than the margin graph method on GPUs. The study also showed that sparse feature maps recover 85% of a graph's squared norm on active features but only 47% when masked to their own graph, with unmasking the inactive tenth nearest the TopK threshold recovering 73% of the masking loss. This indicates that the margin to the TopK threshold largely determines how ablations affect activations and what information graphs carry between different SAE seeds.

entry.title: Report: Anthropic plans IPO amid debates over AI safety and company strategy
entry.summary: Anthropic is preparing for an initial public offering as discussions intensify around its approach to AI safety and the company's future direction. The move highlights ongoing tensions in the AI industry regarding responsible development and commercialization. The IPO could influence how AI safety concerns are addressed by emerging companies and impact investor confidence in the sector.

entry.title: Researchers apply neutrosophic logic via the Jacobian lens to analyze internal epistemic states in Qwen3.5-4B, revealing evidence tracking and belief discrimination across model layers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: This paper presents the first application of neutrosophic logic to internal representations of a large language model, Qwen3.5-4B, using the Jacobian lens to measure truth, indeterminacy, and falsity components across layers. The study identifies distinct signatures such as increased refutation under conflict and sustained indeterminacy under false belief, but finds some effects are artifacts of prompt templates. After controlling for these, the neutrosophic verdict balance reliably tracks evidence polarity and distinguishes false from true first-person beliefs across layers. The authors propose a two-battery protocol for auditing language model internals using lens-based readouts, emphasizing the importance of independent neutrosophic components for measurement and self-correction.

entry.title: Study compares Alzheimer's caregiving advice from peer caregivers, clinicians, ChatGPT, and retrieval-augmented CareGPT across 85 real questions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Researchers analyzed responses to 85 Alzheimer's caregiving questions from four groups: peer caregivers, physicians, ChatGPT, and CareGPT, a retrieval-augmented model based on peer discussions. They assessed differences in linguistic style, emotional and informational support, and topic coverage, finding that peers offered narrative and community-based advice, clinicians gave concise clinical guidance, and large language models (LLMs) provided formal, structured consultations. CareGPT showed little difference from ChatGPT, indicating that retrieval augmentation alone did not change communication style. LLMs scored higher on politeness and emotional support than peers and matched clinicians in informativeness but lacked narrative depth and contextual grounding. Topic analysis revealed LLMs focused on advice-oriented themes, while peers addressed broader issues including emotional, legal, financial, and daily care concerns. The findings suggest AI can complement but not replace human input in Alzheimer's caregiver support, highlighting the potential for hybrid systems that combine AI's structured delivery with the nuanced strengths of human voices.

entry.title: Syntactic Complexity Convergence in Dialogue: Analysis of the Phenomenon and Application to LLM Detection [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.18606v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We revisit the under-explored phenomenon of syntactic complexity convergence in dialogue. Extending prior topic-level analyses to full conversations, we examine five human-human datasets and a set of human-LLM dialogues. We integrate and evaluate a multidimensional set of syntactic complexity metrics to quantify structural variation in dialogue. Our analyses reveal robust syntactic complexity convergence across human-human datasets, especially in task-oriented interactions, and statistical tests confirm that these effects are not due to chance. In contrast, human-LLM dialogues show no significant convergence under individual metrics; however, linear-CKA uncovers a distinct cross-metric convergence pattern. Motivated by these differences, we use syntactic complexity as a feature for detecting LLM-involved dialogue, achieving 96\% accuracy. Our classification results demonstrate its potential without relying on likelihood-based signals such as surprisal, which require a language model as the estimator.

entry.title: Justification of Emotional Appeal in Computational Argumentation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.18607v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Emotional appeals (EAs) are often treated as fallacious in computational argumentation, yet they may be justified when warranted by the context. We introduce the task of predicting EA justification and present the first human-annotated dataset for this task, covering 1,176 argument--context pairs. Grounded in philosophical literature, our framework evaluates EA justification along logical and emotional dimensions. Human annotations show that justification criteria form a shared latent judgment space, with evidential proportionality and normative acceptability most strongly associated with overall justification. We further find that EAs without logical support are not always judged fully unjustified, and stronger EAs are not necessarily judged less justified. Finally, LLM experiments show that EA justification prediction remains challenging.

entry.title: Understanding Failures in LLM Reasoning by Learning Structured Representations of Chain-of-Thought [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.18611v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) is central to improving reasoning in large language models, yet existing evaluation methods focus on step-level signals and ignore the underlying structure of reasoning traces. This raises a key question: what aspects of reasoning quality (i.e., correctness, efficiency, and failure patterns) are encoded in the structure of a CoT trace? We introduce \textbf{CoT2Graph}, a framework that represents CoT traces as directed dependency graphs, making relationships between reasoning steps explicit and capturing patterns such as backtracking, branching, and subtask merging. We model these graphs with graph neural networks and use attribution-based explanations to identify structural patterns associated with reasoning quality. CoT2Graph reveals distinct patterns of successful and failed reasoning: correct CoTs place greater importance on early planning, whereas incorrect CoTs are associated with overloaded synthesis steps and dependency violations. We further show that graph-based signals better predict whether a CoT leads to a correct answer, outperforming previous tree-based structural methods by up to 2.5\% and simple length-based baselines by 7.8\%, while also improving Best-of-$N$ selection. Overall, our results demonstrate that reasoning structure encodes rich signals about reasoning quality, motivating a shift from sequence-level evaluation to structural analysis.

entry.title: When Helpful Agents Cause Financial Harm: Evaluating LLM Agent Safety in Executable Economic Worlds [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.18612v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As LLM agents become increasingly capable of making consequential economic decisions, their safety under economic pressures remains poorly understood. We introduce EconSafeBench, the first benchmark for systematically evaluating the safety of LLM agents in executable economic environments. EconSafeBench contains 828 cases across five economic scenarios and four categories of safety violations. A key design is the matched evaluation of three sources of safety pressure, including explicit user requests, pressure from other actors, and pressure arising from the agent's own pursuit of a performance objective. We further evaluate safety at both static and dynamic scales through 30-period interactions with persistent memory and matched controls. Across eight LLMs, all evaluated models exhibit safety violations on the static benchmark, with overall violation rates ranging from 8.5% to 40.6%. We further find that violations can occur even without an explicit unsafe request, and that initially compliant agents may begin to violate as performance pressure increases over time. These findings highlight the need for stronger safety alignment and rigorous evaluation before LLM agents are deployed in high-stakes economic environments.

entry.title: The Judge Is Not Impartial: Self-Preference in Medical LLM Evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.18616v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to evaluate model-generated medical content, creating a potential circularity: an LLM judge may favor outputs generated by the same model independently of clinical quality. To characterize LLM judge self-preference in medical settings, we measured same-model affinity in single-turn specialist question answering and multi-turn standardized-patient encounters. We evaluated eight models, two from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Qwen, on 620 real point of care questions from clinicians (Real-POCQi). The same eight models also generated and judged 200 standardized patient-clinician scenarios (MedSP1000) up to 8 visible turns. In total, our analysis spans 13,760 LLM judgments. We define three complementary measures of self-preference. Answer Rank Bias, our primary measure, compared the rank assigned to a fixed response by its own-model judge with its average rank from outside judges. Answer Score Bias made the analogous comparison using rubric scores. Own-Answer Win Rate measured how often a judge ranked its own model's response above a competitor. Higher values across all these measures indicate greater degrees of self-preference. In Real-POCQi, pooled Answer Rank Bias was $+1.22$ positions, and all eight judges favored their own answers. Self-preference persisted both with and without a grading rubric. Revealing generator identities modestly weakened self-preference by an average of $-0.094$ positions. In MedSP1000, pooled Answer Rank Bias ranged from $+0.53$ to $+0.62$ positions, with no clear difference by conversation length ($p=0.17$). LLM judges systematically favored responses generated by their own models across multiple formats. Clinical AI deployments should exercise increased vigilance including multiple evaluation measures and judge panels spanning differing model families when deploying LLM-as-a-judge systems.

entry.title: Evaluating the Robustness of Fact-Checking LLMs on Multilingual Evidence [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.18623v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated fact-checking benchmarks typically pair claims with clean, curated evidence in high-resource languages, but real-world evidence is often incomplete, misleading, or written in a language where models are weaker. We evaluate the robustness of fact-checking LLMs for different languages. Building on EuroVerdict, we construct gold evidence sets for 190 claims in each of English, German, Greek, and Romanian, then apply four corruption strategies at two severity levels. We test LLMs on a set of claims, providing them with evidence from the sets above. A rubric-based LLM-as-a-judge scores reasoning quality. Verdict accuracy proves highly sensitive to both factors: Misleading edit cut Llama 3.1 8B's English accuracy from 80.00% to 16.84%, and losses widen as language resource level decreases. Machine-translating Greek and Romanian claims into English recovers much, but not all, of the low-resource gap. Judge scores decline more slowly than accuracy, suggesting that automated reasoning evaluation underestimates degradation. These results caution against deploying LLM fact-checkers on noisy multilingual evidence, and we release our evidence datasets and evaluation code to support future work.

entry.title: Skill Transfer: Adapting Agent Skills from Strong to Weak Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.18624v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent skills are modular bundles of instructions, code, and resources that an agent loads on demand, increasingly authored and validated on frontier models and shared as an open standard. The same skill behaves differently across models: a strong model turns it into a large performance gain, while a weak model realizes little of that gain and sometimes does worse than with no skill at all. Cost and resource constraints, however, often restrict real deployments to exactly these weaker agents. We hypothesize that the strong model silently supplies procedural steps the skill leaves implicit, which the weak model omits, and formalize closing this gap as \emph{Skill Transfer}: holding the skill's capability ceiling and the model's parameters fixed, we adapt the skill so a specific weak agent can execute it well. Our method abstracts strong and weak trajectories into typed execution structures, localizes their structural divergence with a graph edit distance (GED), and repairs the skill through an iterative diagnoser-patcher loop. Across three benchmarks and two model families, Skill Transfer raises pass rate over the unmodified skill significantly and well over other skill-evolution baselines. The adapted skill also improves the strong agent it was never adapted for, and transfers out of distribution to a structurally related, unseen task. Code is available at https://github.com/Yifan-Lan/Skill-Transfer

entry.title: Interpretability-Guided Auditing for Clinical Language Models for Discharge Prediction [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.18626v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clinical natural language processing (NLP) models for hospital discharge prediction are vulnerable to explicit discharge-related lexical cues in clinical notes, even when note timestamps are temporally filtered. These cues may act as proxies for future outcomes, leading models to rely on shortcut-like signals rather than clinically meaningful evidence. We propose AuditBERT-Discharge, a lightweight framework that reframes interpretability as a training-time auditing mechanism. Token-level SHAP attributions from an initial BioClinicalBERT model are used to identify highly attributed discharge-related tokens, which are subsequently masked in the training corpus before model retraining. We evaluate the framework on a retrospective cohort of elective spine surgery encounters from a single academic medical center. Qualitative attribution analysis and preliminary evaluation suggest that SHAP-guided auditing reduces reliance on explicit discharge-proxy language and yields more conservative, better-calibrated predictions, although improvements in discrimination are not uniform. These findings demonstrate the potential of interpretability-guided auditing as a practical strategy for identifying and constraining shortcut-like lexical dependencies in temporally sensitive clinical NLP tasks.

entry.title: FlashREINFORCE: Critic-Free Single-Rollout Asynchronous RL for Agentic Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.18627v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Asynchronous reinforcement learning suits long-horizon agents with irregular rollout times, but group-relative updates require repeated rollouts of each prompt. However, group-based sampling limits prompt coverage at a fixed rollout budget and introduces group synchronization barriers. One rollout per prompt avoids these constraints but removes the variance-reducing group baseline, making updates noisier and more prone to instability on stale, variable-length trajectories. We present FlashREINFORCE, a critic-free, one-pass framework built on One-Batch REINFORCE, a Sequence Trust Region, and Sample-Mean Optimization. These components preserve prompt coverage and signed feedback while controlling policy drift and length-amplified negative updates. In our experiments, FlashREINFORCE remains stable through 6,000 updates on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B at a policy lag of approximately four updates. On Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, it reaches 38.0 mean accuracy across five benchmarks, outperforming the reported GRPO baseline by 1.7 percentage points with half the rollouts (256k versus 512k). Python-tool experiments extend to the 30B MoE model Qwen3-30B-A3B, with stable training at policy lag eight. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, FlashREINFORCE maintains tool use where GRPO stops making tool calls and achieves 98.3%/96.5% seen/unseen ALFWorld success.

entry.title: Wrong with Confidence: Measuring Hallucination, Overconfidence and Identity-Conditioned Behaviour in Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.18728v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models answer underspecified questions readily, and accuracy-only evaluation rewards guessing over abstaining. Observational studies link query underspecification to hallucination, but they cannot separate the effect of missing information from item difficulty, and they rarely ask what the model tells the user. We report a pre-registered, paired behavioural study of five open-weight models (Gemma 3 27B, Gemma 4 31B, gpt-oss-120b, Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B and Nemotron 3 Super). Each of 142 factual questions was posed in a fully specified form and in a referentially underspecified form with the same answer key, and three probes measured identity-conditioned behaviour. Two raters scored 5,620 responses under a fixed rubric; effects were estimated with mixed-effects models. Without the referent, the models sought clarification on 33.7% of prompts and answered the rest. Among attempted answers, the error rate rose from 39.1% to 52.0% (mixed-effects odds ratio 4.12, 95% CI 2.76-6.14), and specialist-domain questions failed more often than general ones in every model. Unelicited verbal uncertainty did not track this risk: 75.3% of wrong answers carried no hedge, wrong answers to underspecified prompts were hedged no more often than wrong answers to clear prompts (27.3% vs 22.3%), and hedging separated correct from incorrect answers only weakly (AUROC 0.56). Gendered pronouns followed occupational stereotypes whenever a model committed to one; any stated user identity lengthened answers by about 45% relative to an anonymous user; claimed expertise did not reduce safety caveats. The models either ask or answer as if the question were well posed, and the wording of a guess does not reveal that it is one. Evaluations should score clarification as a distinct outcome and check label validity as well as rater agreement.

entry.title: KUDEX: A Zero-Shot Decompositional Framework for Logical Analysis in Natural Language [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.18851v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at generating fluent text, they often struggle with multi-step logical reasoning with inferential connections among statements. We introduce KUDEX (Knowledge-Upward-Downward Reasoning Extension), a novel zero-shot, decompositional framework for analyzing and verifying logical relationships in natural language. Unlike traditional approaches that rely on surface-level entailment checks, KUDEX leverages LLMs to decompose reasoning into atomic primitives and constructs transparent reasoning graphs that serve both as execution traces and audit logs. Our framework includes a general prompt adaptation pipeline that adapts to diverse reasoning tasks without additional fine-tuning or domain-specific pipelines. Through comprehensive experiments on benchmarks across four domains, we demonstrate that KUDEX provides superior performance compared to existing methods, offering a more granular and robust framework for assessing logical relationships between statements.

entry.title: SurveyWeave: An Agentic Framework for Automated Survey Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.19029v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Surveys help researchers keep up with fast-moving fields, but they take weeks to months to write. Automated survey generation (AutoSurvey) can alleviate this situation, but it is challenging to draw on hundreds to thousands of precisely scoped papers, choose among many valid structures, and stay faithful to its sources while offering insights. We present SurveyWeave, an agentic architecture that decomposes the problem into four tasks coordinated by three agents, each reviewing others' work and conducting revisions based on feedback. We also introduce WeaveEval, a five-dimension evaluation grounded in prior surveys. A comprehensive comparison shows that SurveyWeave outperforms Codex by 8 points and the strongest AutoSurvey baseline by 6 points.

entry.title: Latency, Speech Recognition and Turn-Taking in Voice Agents for Spanish Phone Negotiation: An Externally Measured Comparison of Pipecat, LiveKit and GPT-Live [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.19118v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A voice agent that negotiates by phone must answer quickly, understand spoken amounts and cope with a caller who talks over it. We compared three architectures for such an agent, negotiating freight rates in Spanish: two cascades (speech recognition, language model and speech synthesis) orchestrated by Pipecat and by LiveKit Agents, and GPT-Live, an OpenAI speech model that listens and speaks without separate stages. A program played the carrier with the same 47 recordings of one speaker for all agents, without the telephone network, in 77 calls per architecture over five negotiation scenarios, and measured latency on the listener's side with a validated instrument. Median latency to the content response was 2,616.0 ms (Pipecat), 3,090.0 ms (LiveKit) and 2,444.8 ms (GPT-Live); the confidence interval of GPT-Live's 171.2 ms advantage over Pipecat includes zero. According to its own timestamps, GPT-Live began to answer 800 ms after the end of the line, close to the 0.8 s published by OpenAI; most of the remaining wait, about 1,367 ms and nearly constant, is the audio's round trip through OpenAI's service. A tool call added 0.9-1.1 s in every architecture, more than any difference between them, and the frameworks' self-reported latency fell short of the listener's wait by 9% (Pipecat) and 22% (LiveKit). Word error rates were low (6.03, 4.93 and 1.47%), but the error on amounts was 13.01% and 12.61% in the cascades, against 2.86% in GPT-Live. With default settings, Pipecat and LiveKit stopped at almost every backchannel and often took it as the carrier's answer: an "ok" spoken over the agent ended in a registered agreement in 3 of 15 Pipecat calls, 2 of 15 LiveKit calls and no GPT-Live call (descriptive counts, not tested). Latency should therefore be measured on the listener's side, and a cascade needs safeguards for spoken amounts and backchannels.

entry.title: MarineSparkLM-4B: A Lightweight Language Model for Marine and Offshore Engineering Built by Parameter-Efficient Adaptation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.19151v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Marine and offshore engineering text is spread across preprints, open-access journals, encyclopedias and institutional documents, and the amount of it is small by pretraining standards. We ask how far a lightweight language model for marine and offshore engineering can be taken with parameter-efficient adaptation on a single workstation-class device. Starting from the 4-billion-parameter OceanGPT-basic-4B-Instruct, we train two independent LoRA adapters, each updating 33.0 million of 4.06 billion parameters (0.81%). Training took 4 hours 40 minutes for the first adapter and 10 minutes for the second on one NVIDIA DGX Spark. The first adapter is trained by next-token prediction on a 61.6-million-token corpus covering ten engineering themes. The corpus was built from 13,879 source documents, of which 7,069 were retained after deduplication and a two-tier keyword filter that removes cross-domain lexical collisions. Its validation loss falls from 2.082 to 1.976 over 1,500 steps. Direct testing showed that this adapter could still drift off topic on a retrieval-grounded ballast-water prompt, so we trained a second adapter on 2,295 question-answer pairs (114 hand-written and 2,181 generated by the base model from corpus passages) with the loss restricted to answer tokens. On 20 held-out prompts scored by hand for accuracy, topicality and specificity (maximum 120), the plain base model, the continuation adapter, the instruction adapter and the instruction adapter with retrieval scored 42, 56, 84 and 88. Absolute accuracy stays low (14 of 40 without retrieval and 20 of 40 with it). We report the full pipeline, two negative results (a reverted keyword fix and an instruction run that overfit within 100 steps), and the limits of the evaluation, which uses one small prompt set, no inter-rater agreement measure and model-generated reference answers.

entry.title: Isolating Perception for Multi-View Planning under Occlusion-Induced Partial Observability [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.19179v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are beginning to saturate visual planning benchmarks, yet they fail to resolve depth ambiguity and degrade sharply with problem size under occlusion-induced partial observability (PO). We introduce BW-PO based on the Blocksworld domain, a controlled benchmark that reduces existing VLM planners and formalizers to near-zero performance, and propose VLM-as-perceiver, a paradigm that narrows the VLM's role to local perception while delegating cross-view evidence reconciliation and plan generation to external solvers. Across model-specific challenging subsets of BW-PO, this raises plan success from 1% to 97% for Gemma-4-31B, 0% to 95% for Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, and 3% to 84% for Gemini-3.1-Pro. Isolating perception in this way separates two bottlenecks that are otherwise entangled: reconciliation under depth ambiguity, and completeness of visual extraction under scene density.

entry.title: Revisiting What Makes a Good Context Subset: A Sparse Latent Basis Perspective [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: arXiv:2611.19220v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Selecting context subsets is increasingly important in modern LLM inference, yet what makes a subset effective remains unclear. We study this question in the controlled setting of few-shot demonstration selection. We examine a hypothesis that demonstrations should collectively provide task-relevant information needed by a target query. Assuming that the query representation provides a useful proxy for these requirements, we formulate selection as sparse reconstruction and instantiate it with Residual Explanation Search (RES), a Matching-Pursuit-style diagnostic procedure. Across seven benchmarks and eight open-weight LLMs, no retrieval objective is universally best. RES outperforms MMR in 34 of 56 model--dataset pairs, with its clearest advantage on sentiment tasks, suggesting that query-conditioned collective reconstruction may capture useful complementarity that pairwise dissimilarity misses. Relevance-based retrieval remains strong on template-heavy reasoning benchmarks, while all retrieval methods underperform zero-shot prediction on average on StrategyQA, where a solution-reconstruction analysis is consistent with the query not exposing the required external knowledge. Target-model hidden states further show that retrieval objectives interact differently with representation spaces: middle-layer representations generally favor similarity retrieval, whereas last-layer representations are often stronger for residual- and diversity-based selection. These findings support a conditional, representation-dependent account of context subset quality rather than a universally superior selector.

entry.title: OmitEHR: Scalable Omission Detection in LLM-Generated Clinical Summaries [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
